lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Saying hello
lessons.body:
Welcome! In this lesson you will learn how to say hello in a friendly, simple way.

Learn these words:
Hello. — A polite hello for any time of day.
Hi. — A friendly, short hello.
Good morning. — Use this in the morning.
Good afternoon. — Use this in the afternoon.
Good evening. — Use this in the evening.
How are you? — A kind question when you meet someone.
I am fine, thank you. — A simple, polite answer.
Nice to meet you. — Say this the first time you meet someone.

Examples:
A: Hello! How are you?
B: I am fine, thank you. And you?
A: I am fine too. Nice to meet you.
B: Nice to meet you too.

Try it: Say hello to one person today. Smile, say 'Hello, how are you?' and listen to the answer. That is a good first step.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Introducing yourself
lessons.body:
In this lesson you will learn how to tell someone your name, where you are from, and where you live now.

Learn these sentences:
My name is Sara. — Say your own name here.
I am from Egypt. — Say the country you are from.
I live in Winnipeg now. — Say the city where you live now.
I speak Arabic and a little English. — Say the languages you speak.
I am new to Canada. — A clear, honest sentence for a first meeting.

Examples:
A: Hello, my name is Omar. What is your name?
B: My name is Lina. Nice to meet you.
A: Nice to meet you too. I am new to Canada.
B: Welcome! I live here in Winnipeg.

Try it: Write three sentences about yourself. 1) My name is ___. 2) I am from ___. 3) I live in ___ now. Say them out loud slowly, two times. It is fine to speak slowly. Clear and slow is good.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Polite words: please, thank you, sorry
lessons.body:
Polite words help a lot in a new place. In this lesson you will learn three small words that make a big difference.

Please — Use it when you ask for something.
Example: Please, can you help me?

Thank you — Use it when someone helps you.
Example: Thank you very much.

Sorry — Use it when you make a small mistake, or when you do not understand.
Example: Sorry, I do not understand. Can you say that again, please?

Excuse me — Use it to get attention in a polite way, or to pass someone in a small space.
Example: Excuse me, where is the bus stop?

Try it: Make one polite question today. For example: 'Excuse me, can you help me, please?' Then say 'Thank you' when the person helps you. These words are useful at school, at work, at a store, and on the bus.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Everyday questions and short answers
lessons.body:
In this lesson you will learn short questions you can use every day, and short answers you can understand easily.

Where is the library? — Ask for a place.
How much is this? — Ask for a price in a store.
What time is it? — Ask for the time.
Do you speak English? — A useful first question. You can also say: I speak a little English.
Can you help me, please? — Ask for help in a polite way.

Short answers:
Yes, please. / No, thank you.
It is over there. — The person shows you with a hand or a direction.
It is ten dollars. — Listen for a number and the word dollars.

Review: Say hello, tell someone your name, say please and thank you, and ask one question. That is the whole course in one short talk. Well done! Practice a little every day. Short practice, every day, is better than long practice one time.

courses.title: Foundation 2 — At home, at school, and in the neighbourhood

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — At home with family
lessons.body: Learn: Home words help you talk about daily life. Say: kitchen, bedroom, bathroom, living room, door, window, table, chair. Family words: mother, father, sister, brother, grandmother, grandfather, baby, friend. Examples: This is my kitchen. My sister is in the bedroom. The door is open. Try it: Point to a room in your home and say its name. Then say one family word and one room word together, for example: My brother is in the living room. More examples: This is my mother. That is our living room. Try it again with a friend: ask, What room is this? and answer with a room word.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — At school: classroom words
lessons.body: Learn: School words help you ask for help and follow a lesson. Say: teacher, student, book, pen, paper, desk, board, bag, lesson, homework. Examples: The teacher is at the board. I have my book and pen. My homework is in my bag. Try it: Make three short sentences with teacher, book, and desk. Then practise this question: Excuse me, teacher, can you help me, please? More examples: The student sits at a desk. The book is on the desk. Try it again: point to your pen and say, This is my pen.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — In the neighbourhood: shops and places
lessons.body: Learn: Neighbourhood words help you find places and ask for directions. Say: shop, library, bus stop, park, bank, clinic, street, corner. Examples: The library is on this street. The bus stop is near the park. I go to the shop in the morning. Try it: Say where you go each week, for example: I go to the library on Monday. Then ask: Excuse me, where is the bus stop, please? More examples: The clinic is across the street. The park is behind the shop. Try it again: ask a friend, Where is the library?

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — My daily routine
lessons.body: Learn: Routine words help you talk about your day in order. Say: morning, afternoon, evening, wake up, eat breakfast, go to school, go to work, come home, sleep. Examples: In the morning, I wake up and eat breakfast. In the afternoon, I go to school. In the evening, I come home. Try it: Tell your day in three sentences, one for morning, one for afternoon, and one for evening. More examples: I wake up at seven. I eat lunch in the afternoon. Try it again: tell a friend your routine for tomorrow.

categories.description: Everyday English for newcomers: greetings, shopping, health, work, and conversation.
categories.name: Foundation and Conversation

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Rooms and things in my home
lessons.body:
Learn: Home words help you talk about where you live. Learn: kitchen, bedroom, bathroom, living room, hall, table, chair, bed, door, window. Use 'This is' and 'There is' to describe a room: This is my kitchen. There is a table in the kitchen.

Examples:
This is my bedroom. There is a bed and a chair.
The window is open. The door is closed.
My family eats in the kitchen.

Try it: Walk through your home and name each room out loud. Then say one sentence for each room, for example: There is a table in the living room.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Food and meals
lessons.body:
Learn: Food words help you cook, shop, and eat with others. Learn: bread, rice, milk, eggs, cheese, fruit, vegetables, chicken, tea, coffee. Use 'I like' and 'I want': I like rice. I want tea, please.

Examples:
I eat bread and eggs for breakfast.
We drink tea in the evening.
I like fruit, but I do not like coffee.

Try it: Say what you eat for breakfast, lunch, and dinner, one sentence for each meal. Then ask a friend: What do you like to eat?

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — My family
lessons.body:
Learn: Family words help you introduce the people close to you. Learn: mother, father, sister, brother, daughter, son, grandmother, grandfather, baby. Use 'This is my' and 'He is' or 'She is': This is my sister. She is a student.

Examples:
This is my brother. His name is Ali.
My mother is a teacher. My father works in a shop.
We have two children: a son and a daughter.

Try it: Introduce your family in four sentences: This is my ___. He/She is ___. Then say one thing each person likes to do.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — My day: morning, afternoon, evening
lessons.body:
Learn: Day words help you talk about your routine in order. Learn: morning, afternoon, evening, night, wake up, eat breakfast, go to school, go to work, come home, sleep. Start with 'In the morning' or 'In the evening'.

Examples:
In the morning, I wake up at seven.
In the afternoon, I go to school.
In the evening, I come home and eat dinner.

Try it: Tell your day in three sentences, one for morning, afternoon, and evening. Say them slowly, then tell them again a little faster.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Taking the bus
lessons.body:
Learn: Bus words help you travel on your own. Learn: bus stop, bus driver, ticket, bus pass, get on, get off, next stop. Ask: Excuse me, does this bus go to the library? Listen for yes, no, and the stop name.

Examples:
I get on the bus at the bus stop near my home.
Excuse me, does this bus go downtown?
I get off at the library stop.

Try it: Practise this question three times: Excuse me, does this bus go to ___? Fill in a real place: the library, the school, or the clinic.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Asking for directions
lessons.body:
Learn: Direction words help you find a place. Learn: left, right, straight, near, far, next to, across from, turn. Use 'Where is' and 'How do I get to': Where is the park? How do I get to the school?

Examples:
Go straight, then turn left.
The park is next to the library.
The school is across from the shop.

Try it: Draw a small map of your street. Point to a place and give directions: Go straight, turn right. Then ask a friend for directions to your home.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Places in my neighbourhood
lessons.body:
Learn: Place words help you say where you go each week. Learn: library, park, school, clinic, bank, shop, community centre, post office. Use 'I go to' and 'on Monday' or 'every week': I go to the library on Monday.

Examples:
I go to the park with my children on Sunday.
The clinic is near the library.
We go to the community centre every week.

Try it: Say three places you go to each week and the day you go. Then ask a friend: Where do you go on Saturday?

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Weather and seasons
lessons.body:
Learn: Weather words help you dress right and make small talk. Learn: sunny, cloudy, rainy, snowy, windy, cold, warm, hot. Use 'It is' and 'Today is': It is cold today. In Canada, winter is cold and snowy, and summer is warm.

Examples:
It is sunny today. I wear a light jacket.
It is snowing. I wear boots and a warm coat.
Tomorrow it will be rainy, so I take an umbrella.

Try it: Look outside and say the weather in one sentence. Then say what you wear today and what the weather is like in your home country.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — In the grocery store
lessons.body:
Learn: Store words help you buy food with confidence. Learn: apples, bananas, bread, milk, rice, eggs, soap, bag. Ask: Where is the bread, please? Say: I want two bags of rice, please. Listen for the price in dollars.

Examples:
Where is the milk, please? It is in aisle three.
I want one bag of apples, please.
Thank you. That is ten dollars.

Try it: Make a shopping list of five foods. Practise asking for each one: Where is the ___, please? Then practise the answer: It is over there.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Prices and paying
lessons.body:
Learn: Price words help you understand and pay. Learn: How much is this? How much are these? dollar, cents, change, cash, card. Say: I pay by card. Ask for change: Can I have my change, please?

Examples:
How much is this bread? It is four dollars.
How much are these apples? They are six dollars.
I pay by card. Thank you.

Try it: Practise prices: pick five things at home and say their price in dollars. Then practise paying: Here is twenty dollars. Thank you.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Clothes and sizes
lessons.body:
Learn: Clothes words help you buy what fits. Learn: shirt, pants, dress, jacket, shoes, hat, gloves, small, medium, large. Ask: Do you have this in medium? Can I try it on, please? Say: It fits well, or: It is too small.

Examples:
Do you have this jacket in large?
Can I try it on, please? Yes, the fitting room is over there.
It fits well. I will take it.

Try it: Say what you are wearing today, piece by piece. Then practise: Do you have this in ___? with small, medium, and large.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — At the checkout: polite phrases
lessons.body:
Learn: Polite phrases make shopping easy and friendly. Learn: Excuse me, please, thank you, sorry, I need a bag, please. At the checkout, the cashier may ask: Do you need a bag? You can answer: Yes, please, or: No, thank you.

Examples:
Excuse me, can you help me, please?
Do you need a bag? Yes, please.
Thank you. Have a nice day! You too.

Try it: Practise a full checkout talk with a friend: greet, ask for a bag, pay, and say thank you. Swap roles and try it again.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Meeting new people
lessons.body:
Learn: Meeting words help you start a friendship. Learn: Hello, Hi, Nice to meet you, What is your name? Where are you from? Say your name slowly and clearly. A smile and a slow, clear voice help a lot.

Examples:
Hello, my name is Sara. What is your name?
My name is Omar. Nice to meet you.
Nice to meet you too. Where are you from?

Try it: Practise meeting someone: say hello, your name, and where you are from. Then ask their name. Do it three times, a little faster each time.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Simple questions and answers
lessons.body:
Learn: Short questions help you every day. Learn: What is this? Where is the library? When is the lesson? Who is that? How are you? Answer in short sentences: It is a book. It is on Main Street. I am fine, thank you.

Examples:
What is this? It is a bus ticket.
Where is the school? It is next to the park.
When is the lesson? It is on Monday at ten.

Try it: Ask a friend five short questions with what, where, when, who, and how. Then answer five questions from your friend.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — On the phone: simple calls
lessons.body:
Learn: Phone words help you make a short, clear call. Learn: Hello, this is ___, May I speak to ___, please? Sorry, I do not understand. Can you say that again, please? Speak slowly, and write down names and times.

Examples:
Hello, this is Sara. May I speak to the teacher, please?
Sorry, I do not understand. Can you say that again, please?
Thank you. Goodbye.

Try it: Practise a phone call: say hello, your name, and one question. Then practise: Sorry, can you say that again, please? It is a very useful sentence.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Saying sorry and asking for help
lessons.body:
Learn: Help words help you when English is hard. Learn: Sorry, I do not understand. Can you help me, please? Can you speak slowly, please? What does this word mean? It is fine to ask. People are usually glad to help.

Examples:
Sorry, I do not understand. Can you speak slowly, please?
Can you help me, please? Yes, of course.
What does this word mean? It means a place to read and study.

Try it: Practise asking for help in three ways: Can you help me? Can you speak slowly? What does this mean? Use them this week in a real situation.

categories.name: English level A1
categories.description: Beginner English: everyday words, simple sentences, and basic conversation.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Renting a home: key words
lessons.body:
Learn: Housing words help you understand your home. Learn: rent, landlord, tenant, lease, apartment, deposit, keys, move in, move out. Your lease is the written agreement for your home. Read it slowly, and ask about any word you do not know.

Examples:
I pay rent on the first day of the month.
My landlord gave me the keys on moving day.
Our lease is for one year.

Try it: Write three sentences about your home: how many rooms, what floor, and when you moved in. Use rent, lease, and landlord in your sentences.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Asking for a repair
lessons.body:
Learn: Repair words help you tell your landlord about a problem. Learn: broken, leaking, not working, tap, heater, light, lock. Be clear and polite: Hello, the tap in the kitchen is leaking. Can you fix it, please?

Examples:
Hello, the heater in the bedroom is not working.
The lock on the front door is broken.
Can you send someone to fix it, please? Thank you.

Try it: Write a short repair message: say what is broken, where it is, and when you saw it. Keep it polite and clear, in three or four sentences.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Living with neighbours
lessons.body:
Learn: Neighbour words help you live well in a building. Learn: neighbour, quiet hours, shared laundry, garbage, recycling, hallway. Be friendly: say hello, keep noise down in the evening, and put garbage in the right bin.

Examples:
My neighbours are friendly. We say hello in the hallway.
Please keep quiet after ten in the evening.
We put recycling in the blue bin.

Try it: Write three good-neighbour rules for your building. Then practise a friendly greeting: Hello, how are you? I am your new neighbour.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Moving and changing address
lessons.body:
Learn: Moving words help you plan a move. Learn: moving day, boxes, moving company, new address, change my address, mail. Tell your bank, your school, and your landlord your new address, and ask the post office about mail forwarding.

Examples:
We are moving on Saturday. We have ten boxes.
Please change my address to 45 King Street.
I told my bank and my children's school.

Try it: Write a short moving list: five things to do before moving day. Then write one sentence telling someone your new address.

courses.title: A2 — Work and job search basics

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Jobs and workplaces
lessons.body:
Learn: Job words help you talk about work. Learn: job, workplace, boss, coworker, shift, full-time, part-time, salary, break. Use present simple: I work in a shop. I work from nine to five. My boss is kind.

Examples:
I work part-time in a restaurant.
My shift starts at eight in the morning.
My coworkers help me when I have a question.

Try it: Say where you work or want to work, your hours, and one thing you like about the job. Use three sentences, all in present simple.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Writing a simple resume
lessons.body:
Learn: A resume is a short list of your skills and past jobs. Learn: name, phone number, email, experience, skills, education, languages. Write clearly: one job per line, with the place and the dates. Keep it to one page if you can.

Examples:
Name: Sara Ahmed. Phone: 204-555-0134.
Experience: Cook, Sunrise Restaurant, 2023–2025.
Languages: Arabic, English. Skills: cooking, teamwork.

Try it: Write your own simple resume: name, contact, two jobs or skills, and languages. Ask a friend or teacher to read it and check for mistakes.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — A simple job interview
lessons.body:
Learn: Interview words help you answer with confidence. Learn: Tell me about yourself. Why do you want this job? What are your strengths? Practise short answers: I am hardworking. I like helping customers. I learn quickly.

Examples:
Tell me about yourself. I worked in a shop for two years.
Why do you want this job? I like working with people.
Thank you for the interview. I look forward to hearing from you.

Try it: Practise answering three interview questions out loud. Keep each answer to two or three sentences. Then practise asking: When will you decide?

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — At work: polite requests
lessons.body:
Learn: Polite requests help you at work every day. Learn: Could you help me, please? Can I ask a question? Sorry, I did not understand. Could you show me again, please? Say thank you when a coworker helps you.

Examples:
Could you help me with this box, please?
Sorry, I did not understand. Could you say that again, please?
Can I take my break now? Yes, of course.

Try it: Practise four polite requests for work: asking for help, asking a question, asking to repeat, and asking for a break. Say each one twice.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Parts of the body and symptoms
lessons.body:
Learn: Body words help you explain how you feel. Learn: head, stomach, back, arm, leg, throat, tooth, fever, cough, headache, stomachache. Say: I have a headache. My back hurts. I feel sick.

Examples:
I have a cough and a sore throat.
My stomach hurts. I feel sick.
Her arm hurts. She needs to see a doctor.

Try it: Point to five parts of your body and name each one. Then say: I have a ___ and My ___ hurts, with two real or practice examples.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Booking a doctor's appointment
lessons.body:
Learn: Appointment words help you see a doctor. Learn: appointment, clinic, doctor, nurse, health card, available, morning, afternoon. Say: Hello, I would like to book an appointment, please. Bring your health card with you.

Examples:
Hello, I would like to book an appointment with Dr. Lee, please.
Are you available on Thursday morning?
Yes, Thursday at ten. Please bring your health card.

Try it: Practise booking an appointment by phone: greet, ask for an appointment, say a day and time, and confirm: So, Thursday at ten. Thank you.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — At the pharmacy
lessons.body:
Learn: Pharmacy words help you get medicine safely. Learn: pharmacy, pharmacist, prescription, medicine, tablets, dose, once a day, twice a day, before meals. Always ask: How do I take this medicine? Listen carefully to the answer.

Examples:
I have a prescription from my doctor.
How do I take this medicine? Take one tablet twice a day.
Do I take it before meals? Yes, before breakfast and dinner.

Try it: Practise asking a pharmacist three questions: How do I take this? How many times a day? Before or after meals? Write the answers in your notebook.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — When to get urgent help
lessons.body:
Learn: Urgent words help you in an emergency. Learn: emergency, ambulance, hospital, emergency room, I need help, It hurts a lot. In Canada, call 911 for a serious emergency. Stay calm, give your address, and say what happened.

Examples:
I need help. My friend fell and cannot stand up.
Please call an ambulance. We are at 45 King Street.
Stay on the phone. Help is on the way.

Try it: Practise saying your address clearly, three times. Then practise an emergency sentence: I need help. Please call an ambulance. We are at ___.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Talking to your child's teacher
lessons.body:
Learn: School words help you support your child. Learn: teacher, classroom, homework, report card, parent-teacher meeting, progress. Ask: How is my child doing? What can we practise at home? Thank the teacher at the end.

Examples:
Hello, I am Sara's mother. How is Sara doing in class?
She is doing well. She reads every day.
Thank you. What can we practise at home?

Try it: Write three questions for a parent-teacher meeting. Practise asking them politely, and practise saying: Thank you for your help.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Reading school notes and letters
lessons.body:
Learn: School notes tell you about trips, meetings, and holidays. Learn: field trip, permission form, school holiday, early dismissal, sign, return by. Read the date first, then the action: sign the form, return it by Friday.

Examples:
There is a field trip on Friday, May 8.
Please sign the permission form and return it by Wednesday.
School closes early on Thursday at two.

Try it: Read a school note slowly and find: the date, the place, and what parents must do. Write the three answers in your notebook.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Homework and studying at home
lessons.body:
Learn: Homework words help your child learn at home. Learn: homework, read aloud, practise, spelling, math, project, due. Make a quiet time each day: thirty minutes for homework, then a break. Praise effort, not only correct answers.

Examples:
My son does his homework after dinner.
Please read this page aloud, then practise the spelling words.
The project is due on Monday.

Try it: Make a homework plan with your child: a time, a place, and a short break. Write it in three sentences and put it on the fridge.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — School routines and absences
lessons.body:
Learn: Routine words help you tell the school about your child. Learn: absent, sick, late, excuse, school office, call the school. If your child is sick, call the school in the morning: Hello, my daughter Sara is sick today. She will stay home.

Examples:
Hello, this is Sara's father. Sara is sick today.
She will not come to school. Thank you.
Please call the school office if your child will be late.

Try it: Practise an absence call: your name, your child's name, the reason, and thank you. Keep it short and clear, under thirty seconds.

categories.name: English level A2
categories.description: Elementary English: everyday life, work, and simple past and future sentences.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Understanding your lease
lessons.body:
Learn: A lease sets out rent, rules, and responsibilities. Read it before you sign: how much is the rent, when is it due, how long is the term, and what happens if you need to leave early? If a sentence is unclear, ask for an explanation in writing and keep a copy of everything you sign.

Examples:
The rent is $1,200 per month, due on the first.
The lease term is twelve months, from May 1 to April 30.
The tenant must give notice in writing before moving out.

Try it: Read one section of a sample lease and write down three facts: the rent, the term, and one rule. Then write one question you would ask the landlord.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Writing to your landlord
lessons.body:
Learn: A clear written message protects both sides. Start politely, state the problem and the date, say what you need, and keep a copy. Example opening: Dear Ms. Lee, I am writing about the leaking tap in the kitchen, first noticed on March 3. Could you please arrange a repair?

Examples:
Dear Mr. Chen, I am writing about the broken heater in the bedroom.
It stopped working on January 12. Could you please send someone this week?
Thank you for your help. Sara Ahmed, Unit 12.

Try it: Write a short message to a landlord about a repair: greeting, problem and date, request, and thanks. Keep it under ten sentences and check your spelling.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Giving notice and moving out
lessons.body:
Learn: When you plan to leave, notice rules matter. Most leases ask for written notice a set time before the end of the term, often one or two months. State your name, unit, and last day clearly, and ask for a move-out inspection and the return of your deposit in writing.

Examples:
Dear landlord, I am giving notice that I will move out on June 30.
My name is Omar Hassan, Unit 211.
Could we arrange a move-out inspection, please?

Try it: Write a notice message with your name, unit, and moving date. Then list three things to do on moving day: clean, return keys, and take photos of the rooms.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Where to get help with housing
lessons.body:
Learn: If a housing problem is not solved, you do not have to face it alone. Settlement agencies, tenant associations, and community legal clinics can explain your rights and help you write letters. Bring your lease, photos, and copies of messages to your appointment.

Examples:
I have a problem with a repair. Can you help me understand my rights?
Please bring your lease and photos to the appointment.
The clinic helped me write a letter to my landlord.

Try it: Find one local settlement or tenant help service and write down its name, address, and phone number. Practise explaining your problem in three sentences.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Searching for jobs
lessons.body:
Learn: A good job search uses several routes: online job boards, employment centres, settlement agencies, and people you know. Read each posting carefully: the duties, the hours, the location, and how to apply. Apply only for jobs you can really do, and keep a list of where you applied.

Examples:
I found this job on a job board. The hours are full-time, Monday to Friday.
The posting asks for two years of experience and good English.
I applied on Tuesday and wrote the date in my list.

Try it: Find one real job posting and write down the job title, duties, hours, and how to apply. Then write one sentence explaining why the job fits you.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Writing a cover letter
lessons.body:
Learn: A cover letter explains why you want a job and what you offer. Keep it short: one paragraph about the job, one about your experience, and one closing line. Use the job title and the company name, and end with: Thank you for considering my application.

Examples:
Dear hiring manager, I am applying for the cook position at Sunrise Restaurant.
I have three years of experience in busy kitchens and I work well in a team.
Thank you for considering my application. I look forward to hearing from you.

Try it: Write a short cover letter for a job you would like: three paragraphs, each two or three sentences. Ask a friend to check it for clear, polite language.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Answering interview questions
lessons.body:
Learn: Strong interview answers use real examples. For 'Tell me about a challenge', describe the situation, what you did, and the result, in that order. Speak slowly, listen to the full question, and do not be afraid to pause before answering.

Examples:
Tell me about a difficult day at work. One busy evening, two cooks were sick.
I organized the orders and helped at two stations.
We served every customer on time, and my manager thanked me.

Try it: Prepare answers for three questions: about yourself, a challenge, and teamwork. Practise each answer out loud in under one minute.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Starting a new job well
lessons.body:
Learn: The first weeks at a new job are for learning. Ask about safety rules, break times, and who to ask when you are unsure. Write down new words and procedures, arrive on time, and tell your supervisor early if you do not understand a task.

Examples:
On my first day, my supervisor showed me the safety rules.
I wrote down the break times and the name of my trainer.
If I do not understand, I ask: Could you show me again, please?

Try it: Write five questions to ask on your first day at a new job: about safety, breaks, duties, training, and who to ask for help.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Finding a family doctor
lessons.body:
Learn: A family doctor knows your health history and can refer you to specialists. Ask a settlement agency, a clinic, or friends for names, and check whether the doctor is accepting new patients. Bring your health card and a list of medicines to your first visit.

Examples:
Hello, is Dr. Lee accepting new patients?
I am new to Winnipeg and I need a family doctor.
My first appointment is on Tuesday. I will bring my health card.

Try it: Write a short phone script for finding a doctor: greeting, your situation, the question about new patients, and thanks. Practise it out loud twice.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Walk-in clinics and emergencies
lessons.body:
Learn: Walk-in clinics help when you cannot see your family doctor soon. For a serious emergency, such as trouble breathing or heavy bleeding, call 911 or go to the emergency room. For a minor problem, a walk-in clinic or pharmacist can often help first.

Examples:
My doctor is away this week, so I went to a walk-in clinic.
I waited one hour and saw a doctor about my cough.
If it is an emergency, call 911. Do not drive yourself.

Try it: Write two situations: one for a walk-in clinic and one for 911. Explain your choice in one sentence for each, and share them with a friend.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Understanding prescriptions
lessons.body:
Learn: A prescription tells you the medicine, the dose, and how often to take it. Read the label: the patient's name, the drug name, the dose, and the directions. Ask the pharmacist if anything is unclear, and never share prescription medicine with another person.

Examples:
Take one tablet in the morning and one at night.
Finish all the tablets, even if you feel better.
If you feel dizzy, call the pharmacy and ask for advice.

Try it: Read a sample medicine label and write down the drug name, dose, and directions. Then write two questions you would ask the pharmacist.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Mental health and community support
lessons.body:
Learn: Settling in a new country can be stressful, and asking for help is a sign of strength. Community centres, settlement agencies, and health clinics can connect you with counselling and support groups. Talking with someone you trust, keeping a routine, and getting outside can also help.

Examples:
Since moving here, I have felt lonely and worried.
A counsellor at the settlement agency helped me make a plan.
I joined a conversation group and I feel better now.

Try it: Write three things that help you feel calm, and one person or service you could talk to if you feel stressed. Keep this list somewhere you can find it.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Using the bank
lessons.body:
Learn: Bank words help you manage money safely. Learn: account, savings, chequing, debit card, PIN, deposit, withdraw, statement, branch. Never share your PIN with anyone, and check your statement each month for transactions you do not recognize.

Examples:
I would like to open a chequing account, please.
I deposit my paycheque every two weeks.
Please do not share your PIN, even with family.

Try it: Practise a bank visit: greet, ask to open an account, and ask what documents you need. Write down the documents you must bring.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — The public library
lessons.body:
Learn: Libraries are free and open to everyone. You can borrow books, use computers, study, and join free programs, including conversation groups and help with resumes. Ask staff for a library card: bring identification and proof of address.

Examples:
I would like a library card, please. Here is my identification.
You can borrow books for three weeks.
The conversation group meets every Thursday at six.

Try it: Visit a library or its website and write down three free services it offers. Then write one question you would ask library staff.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Community centres and programs
lessons.body:
Learn: Community centres offer sports, classes, childcare programs, and events for all ages. Many programs are free or low-cost for newcomers. Ask about registration, schedules, and whether you need to bring anything, such as indoor shoes or a water bottle.

Examples:
The community centre has swimming lessons for children on Saturdays.
Registration opens on Monday. Please bring a swimsuit and towel.
I joined a cooking class and met three new friends.

Try it: Find one program at a community centre near you and write down its name, day, time, and cost. Then tell a friend why you would like to join.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Volunteering in your community
lessons.body:
Learn: Volunteering means giving time to help others, and it is a good way to practise English, meet people, and gain Canadian experience. Food banks, libraries, schools, and festivals all need volunteers. Ask: What tasks do volunteers do, and how many hours per week?

Examples:
I volunteer at the food bank every Saturday morning.
I sort food donations and greet visitors.
Volunteering helped my English and my confidence.

Try it: Write three places where you could volunteer and one skill you could offer each place. Then write a short message asking about volunteering.

categories.name: English level B1
categories.description: Intermediate English: longer conversations, opinions, and everyday problems.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Writing professional emails
lessons.body:
Learn: A professional email is short, clear, and polite. Use a clear subject line, a greeting, one main point per paragraph, and a polite closing. Avoid slang and all-caps, and re-read before sending, especially names, dates, and attachments.

Examples:
Subject: Request for Friday shift change
Dear Ms. Patel, I am writing to ask if I can swap my Friday shift with Sam's.
I have a medical appointment that morning. Thank you for considering this. Best regards, Sara.

Try it: Write an email asking for a schedule change: subject line, greeting, reason, request, and closing. Keep it under 120 words and re-read it before finishing.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Speaking up in meetings
lessons.body:
Learn: Meetings work better when everyone contributes. Use phrases to join in politely: 'May I add something?' 'I agree, and I would add...' 'Sorry, could you explain that point?' Prepare one point before the meeting, and listen carefully before responding.

Examples:
May I add something to that idea? I think customers would like longer hours.
I agree with Ali, and I would add that weekend hours matter most.
Sorry, could you explain the new schedule again?

Try it: Prepare one point for a practice meeting and express it in three ways: agreeing, adding an idea, and asking for clarification.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Giving and receiving feedback
lessons.body:
Learn: Good feedback is specific, kind, and focused on actions, not people. When you receive feedback, listen fully, thank the person, and ask a clarifying question instead of defending yourself at once. Then decide what you will change and follow up.

Examples:
Your report was clear, and adding a summary would make it stronger.
Thank you for the feedback. Could you show me an example?
I will add a short summary to the next report.

Try it: Practise giving feedback on a sample report: one strength, one suggestion, and one question. Then practise receiving feedback without interrupting.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Workplace safety conversations
lessons.body:
Learn: Safety talk must be clear, even when it feels awkward. Report hazards right away, ask about protective equipment, and confirm instructions: 'So I should wear gloves and goggles for this task, correct?' If a task feels unsafe, stop and ask your supervisor before continuing.

Examples:
I noticed the floor is wet near the entrance. I will put up a sign.
Do I need gloves for this cleaning product?
I am not sure this ladder is safe. Could you check it, please?

Try it: Write three safety sentences for your workplace: reporting a hazard, asking about equipment, and confirming an instruction. Practise saying them clearly.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Your Social Insurance Number
lessons.body:
Learn: A Social Insurance Number, or SIN, is needed to work in Canada and to access government programs. Apply through Service Canada with your immigration documents. Keep your SIN private: share it only with your employer, your bank, and government agencies that need it.

Examples:
I applied for my SIN at Service Canada with my work permit.
My employer asked for my SIN on my first day.
I keep my SIN card in a safe place and I do not share it online.

Try it: Write a checklist for a SIN appointment: documents to bring, questions to ask, and where you will store your SIN safely afterwards.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Health cards and identification
lessons.body:
Learn: Each province issues its own health card, and you usually need proof of identity and address to apply. Carry your health card to medical appointments, and report a lost card promptly. Keep copies of important documents in a safe place, separate from the originals.

Examples:
I applied for my Manitoba health card with my passport and lease.
The card arrived by mail in four weeks.
I keep a photocopy at home and the original in my wallet.

Try it: List the documents you used, or would use, to apply for a health card. Then write what you would do first if your card were lost.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Understanding taxes simply
lessons.body:
Learn: Most workers in Canada file a tax return each spring for the previous year. Your employer gives you a T4 slip showing your income and taxes paid. Free community tax clinics can help newcomers file, and filing on time matters even if your income was low.

Examples:
I received my T4 in February. It shows my income for last year.
A volunteer at the tax clinic helped me file my return.
I filed before the deadline, even though my income was small.

Try it: Explain taxes to a friend in five sentences: what a T4 is, when to file, where to get help, and why filing matters. Keep the language simple.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Filling in forms accurately
lessons.body:
Learn: Forms ask for exact information, so copy names and numbers carefully from your documents, not from memory. If a question does not apply, write 'N/A' rather than leaving it blank, and check dates in the order the form asks for: day, month, year, or month, day, year.

Examples:
Please print your full legal name exactly as it appears on your passport.
If you have no middle name, write N/A in that box.
Date of birth: please write day, month, then year.

Try it: Practise filling in a sample form with your name, address, and phone number. Then swap with a friend and check each other's work for errors.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Choosing an adult course
lessons.body:
Learn: Before choosing a course, ask about the goal, the level, the schedule, the cost, and the certificate. A good course matches your goal: a language course for daily life, a certificate course for a job, or a bridging program for your profession. Ask former students what they thought.

Examples:
I want a course that prepares me for work in health care.
The course runs Tuesday and Thursday evenings for twelve weeks.
It costs $200, and there is help for newcomers with low income.

Try it: Choose a real course and write down its goal, level, schedule, cost, and certificate. Then write one sentence explaining why it fits your goal.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Getting credentials recognized
lessons.body:
Learn: If you studied or worked abroad, credential recognition can help employers understand your qualifications. Start by asking a settlement agency which assessment service fits your field. Gather transcripts, diplomas, and work references, and allow several months for the process.

Examples:
I was an engineer in my home country and I want to work here.
The agency advised me to get my degree assessed first.
I gathered my transcripts and two work references.

Try it: List the documents you would need for a credential assessment in your field. Then write three questions to ask an advisor about the process.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Study skills for busy adults
lessons.body:
Learn: Busy adults learn best in short, regular sessions. Study for twenty-five minutes, take a five-minute break, and review the next day. Use real materials: a work email, a school note, or a news article. Teach what you learned to someone else to check your understanding.

Examples:
I study English for thirty minutes after dinner, four days a week.
I read one news article and write down five new words.
On Sunday, I explain the week's ideas to my friend.

Try it: Make a study plan for one week: four short sessions, the materials you will use, and one review day. Keep it realistic for your work and family life.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Presenting in class or at work
lessons.body:
Learn: A good short presentation has a clear start, two or three main points, and a clear ending. Open with your topic and why it matters, speak slowly, look at your audience, and end with a summary and a question. Practise out loud at least twice before the real talk.

Examples:
Good morning. Today I will talk about recycling in our building.
First, I will explain the bins. Second, I will show the schedule.
In summary, recycling helps our building and our city. Any questions?

Try it: Prepare a two-minute talk on a topic you know well: opening, two points, and a closing. Practise it out loud and time yourself.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Reading the news in English
lessons.body:
Learn: News articles usually answer who, what, where, when, and why in the first paragraph. Read the headline and first paragraph first, then look for key facts. Unknown words matter less than the main idea: guess from context, then check only the words that block understanding.

Examples:
The city will open a new library downtown next spring.
The headline says: New library planned for downtown.
I did not know one word, but I understood the main idea.

Try it: Read a short news article and write down the five W answers: who, what, where, when, and why. Then write the main idea in one sentence.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Giving your opinion politely
lessons.body:
Learn: Opinions land better with reasons and polite language. Use: 'In my opinion...', 'I think... because...', and 'I see your point, but...'. Give one reason, not five, and listen to the reply before answering. Disagreeing respectfully is a normal part of discussion.

Examples:
In my opinion, public transit should run later at night, because many people work evening shifts.
I see your point, but later buses also cost more.
That is a fair point. Perhaps weekend service could come first.

Try it: Write your opinion on a local topic with one reason. Then write a polite reply to someone who disagrees, starting with: I see your point, but...

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Discussing a local issue
lessons.body:
Learn: Local issues, like a new bus route or a park closure, affect daily life. Before a discussion, learn the facts: what is proposed, who decides, and when. Present facts first, then your view, and ask others what they think. A discussion is not a debate to win.

Examples:
The city proposes closing the park for repairs in July.
I think the work is needed, but families need another play area.
What do you think? Would a temporary playground help?

Try it: Pick a local issue and write a discussion opener: one fact, your view with a reason, and a question for others. Practise it with a friend.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Checking facts before sharing
lessons.body:
Learn: Before sharing news online, pause and check: who published it, when, and whether another reliable source reports the same story. Headlines can mislead, photos can be old, and a single post is not proof. Sharing only checked stories protects your friends and your reputation.

Examples:
This post claims a new rule, but no news site reports it.
The photo is from 2019, not from this week.
I will not share it until I find a reliable source.

Try it: Take a surprising post you have seen and check it: source, date, and a second source. Write one sentence about what you found and whether you would share it.

categories.name: English level B2
categories.description: Upper-intermediate English: work, study, and detailed discussion in English.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Formal emails that get results
lessons.body:
Learn: Formal emails respect the reader's time. State your purpose in the first sentence, give only the details needed for a decision, and end with a clear next step and a deadline if one exists. A respectful tone matters more than long, complex sentences: clarity is professionalism.

Examples:
Dear Ms. Thompson, I am writing to confirm our meeting on Thursday, May 14, at 10 a.m.
Please let me know if that time still works for you.
If I do not hear from you by Wednesday, I will assume the meeting is confirmed.

Try it: Rewrite a vague email into a formal one: purpose first, necessary details only, and a clear next step. Compare the two versions and note what improved.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Writing clear reports
lessons.body:
Learn: A clear report answers three questions: what happened, what it means, and what should happen next. Use headings, short paragraphs, and a summary at the start. Support claims with numbers or examples, and separate facts from recommendations so readers can judge each part.

Examples:
Summary: Customer complaints fell by 20% after the new schedule began.
Finding: Most complaints concerned evening wait times.
Recommendation: Add one evening staff member on Fridays and Saturdays.

Try it: Write a one-page report on a familiar topic: summary, two findings with evidence, and one recommendation. Ask a colleague to check whether the recommendation follows from the findings.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Presenting to a professional audience
lessons.body:
Learn: Professional presentations persuade through structure, not volume. Open with the problem and your main message, support it with two or three pieces of evidence, and close by stating the decision you need. Anticipate one hard question and prepare an honest answer, including what you do not yet know.

Examples:
Our delivery times have risen by 15% this quarter.
Two causes explain most delays: staffing gaps and a new route.
I recommend hiring one driver and reviewing the route this month.

Try it: Prepare a five-minute presentation: problem, main message, evidence, and a requested decision. Practise answering one difficult question honestly.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Handling difficult conversations
lessons.body:
Learn: Difficult conversations go better with preparation and respect. Describe the situation factually, explain its effect, and invite the other person's view before proposing a solution. Avoid blame language such as 'you always', and focus on a shared goal both sides can accept.

Examples:
I noticed the last two reports arrived after the deadline, which delayed the team's work.
Can you tell me what made those weeks difficult?
Let us agree on a new deadline process that works for both of us.

Try it: Plan a difficult conversation: facts, effect, an open question, and a proposed solution. Role-play it with a friend, then swap roles.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Reading for the main argument
lessons.body:
Learn: Strong readers look past details to find the author's main claim and the evidence behind it. Ask: What is the author trying to convince me of? What evidence is offered? What evidence is missing? A text can be well written and still rest on weak evidence.

Examples:
The article claims the new program will cut waiting times in half.
Its evidence is one short trial in a single clinic.
The article does not discuss cost, staffing, or larger trials.

Try it: Read an opinion article and write its main claim, its best evidence, and one important piece of missing evidence, each in a single sentence.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Recognizing bias and framing
lessons.body:
Learn: Bias often hides in word choice and in what a text leaves out. Compare how two outlets report the same event: which facts each one leads with, which voices each quotes, and which words describe the same people. Framing changes impressions even when the facts overlap.

Examples:
One headline calls the group 'protesters', the other calls them 'residents'.
One article quotes officials first; the other quotes families first.
Both report the same meeting, but readers may reach different conclusions.

Try it: Compare two reports of one event and note three framing differences: headline words, first voice quoted, and one fact only one report includes.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Evaluating sources
lessons.body:
Learn: Not all sources carry equal weight. Check the author, the publisher, the date, and whether claims link to original data. A government statistics release, a peer-reviewed study, and an anonymous post differ greatly in reliability, even when they discuss the same topic.

Examples:
The claim comes from a national statistics release dated last month.
It links to the full data tables, which I checked.
The anonymous post gives no source, so I will not rely on it.

Try it: Evaluate three sources on one topic: author, publisher, date, and evidence. Rank them by reliability and write one sentence justifying your ranking.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Summarizing without distorting
lessons.body:
Learn: A fair summary keeps the author's meaning, including limits and uncertainty. Keep the main claim, drop examples, and preserve words like 'may', 'suggests', or 'in some cases'. A summary that turns a cautious finding into a certainty has distorted the original.

Examples:
Original: The study suggests the program may help some students.
Fair summary: A study suggests the program may help some students.
Distorted summary: The program helps students. This drops may and some.

Try it: Summarize a short article in three sentences without dropping its cautions. Then check: does your summary claim more than the original?

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Speaking at a public meeting
lessons.body:
Learn: Public meetings give residents a voice in decisions. Prepare a short statement: who you are, the issue in one sentence, your experience or evidence, and a specific request. Speak slowly, stay within the time limit, and thank the chair when you finish.

Examples:
Good evening. My name is Sara Ahmed and I live on King Street.
The proposed bus change would remove evening service our shift workers rely on.
I ask the council to keep at least one evening bus. Thank you.

Try it: Write a two-minute statement for a public meeting on a local issue: introduction, issue, evidence, and a specific request. Time yourself reading it.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Writing a proposal
lessons.body:
Learn: A proposal turns an idea into action. State the problem, the proposed solution, the people it helps, the resources needed, and how success will be measured. Decision-makers respond to specific, realistic plans more than to general complaints or praise.

Examples:
Problem: Newcomer parents lack evening conversation practice.
Proposal: A weekly two-hour conversation group at the library.
Resources: One room, two volunteers, and printed materials. Success: Twenty regular participants after three months.

Try it: Write a one-page proposal for a community idea: problem, solution, resources, and one measure of success. Keep each section to three sentences.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Building a coalition
lessons.body:
Learn: Big changes need allies. A coalition brings together people and groups who share a goal but bring different strengths: a school, a faith group, a business, a settlement agency. Agree on a shared goal early, divide tasks clearly, and keep communication regular and respectful.

Examples:
Our goal is a safe crossing near the school.
The parents' group will gather signatures, the school will write a letter, and the community centre will host a meeting.
We meet every two weeks and share notes after each meeting.

Try it: Choose a community goal and list four potential allies and what each could contribute. Then write a short invitation message to one of them.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Negotiating with officials
lessons.body:
Learn: Negotiation with officials works best when you understand their limits. Learn what they can decide, what budget or rules bind them, and what alternatives exist. Ask open questions, propose options rather than ultimatums, and confirm any agreement in writing afterwards.

Examples:
I understand the budget is fixed this year.
Would a pilot project in one neighbourhood be possible instead?
Thank you. I will send a written summary of what we agreed today.

Try it: Prepare for a negotiation: your goal, your best alternative, two options you could accept, and three questions about the official's limits.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Structuring an essay
lessons.body:
Learn: A strong essay has a clear thesis, organized paragraphs, and a conclusion that answers the question. Each paragraph should make one point, support it with evidence or an example, and connect to the next idea. An introduction that promises what the essay delivers keeps readers oriented.

Examples:
Thesis: Libraries deserve evening funding because they serve workers, students, and newcomers.
Each paragraph defends one group with evidence.
The conclusion returns to the thesis and states the funding request.

Try it: Outline an essay on a topic you care about: thesis, three paragraph points with evidence, and a conclusion. Write the introduction paragraph only.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Cover letters for professional roles
lessons.body:
Learn: A professional cover letter connects your experience to the employer's needs, not just your history. Research the organization, name the role, and show two achievements with results. Close by stating what you would bring to the team and requesting an interview.

Examples:
Dear hiring committee, I am applying for the community health worker position.
In my last role, I supported 40 newcomer families and cut missed appointments by 30%.
I would bring settlement experience and strong community links to your team.

Try it: Write a cover letter for a professional role: research the organization first, then connect two of your achievements to its needs in under 300 words.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Writing a formal complaint
lessons.body:
Learn: A formal complaint states facts, dates, and the outcome you seek, without anger or exaggeration. Begin with your account details, describe events in order, attach copies of evidence, and state a reasonable deadline for a reply. Keep a copy of everything you send.

Examples:
Dear Sir or Madam, I am writing to complain about a billing error on account 8841.
On March 2, I was charged $60 for a service I cancelled on February 10.
I ask you to correct the bill and confirm in writing within 14 days.

Try it: Write a formal complaint about a fictional billing error: details, events in order, evidence, and a requested outcome with a deadline. Keep the tone calm throughout.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Editing and proofreading your work
lessons.body:
Learn: Good writing is revised writing. After drafting, rest, then read aloud to catch awkward sentences. Check one thing at a time: first ideas and order, then paragraph links, then grammar and spelling. Reading backwards, sentence by sentence, helps you spot errors your eyes otherwise skip.

Examples:
First draft: The meeting was good and people said things about the plan.
Revised: The meeting produced two decisions: a new schedule and a volunteer list.
The revision names the decisions instead of describing the meeting vaguely.

Try it: Take a paragraph you wrote and revise it twice: once for clarity of ideas, once for grammar. Compare all three versions and keep the clearest one.

categories.name: English level C1
categories.description: Advanced English: clear, detailed English for work and study.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Idioms in everyday Canadian speech
lessons.body:
Learn: Idioms mean more than their words suggest, and Canadians use them constantly. 'Under the weather' means slightly ill, 'break the ice' means ease the start of a conversation, and 'on the same page' means in agreement. Learn idioms in context, not in lists, and notice whether they suit formal or casual settings.

Examples:
I am feeling under the weather today, so I will stay home.
Let us break the ice with introductions before the meeting.
Before we decide, let us make sure we are all on the same page.

Try it: Collect five idioms you hear this week, note where you heard each one, and write one sentence using each idiom correctly in context.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Tone and register
lessons.body:
Learn: Register is the level of formality you choose for a situation. You write to a friend differently than to a judge, a boss, or a stranger. Tone adds attitude: the same request can sound warm, neutral, or demanding depending on word choice and phrasing. Skilled speakers adjust both deliberately.

Examples:
Casual: Hey, can you send that file when you get a chance?
Professional: Could you please send the file at your earliest convenience?
Both ask the same thing, but the register fits a different relationship.

Try it: Rewrite one message in three registers: to a close friend, to a coworker, and to a government office. Note which words changed and why.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Humour and indirect language
lessons.body:
Learn: Canadian humour often uses understatement and gentle irony: saying 'not bad' can mean 'very good', and 'a bit chilly' can mean freezing cold. Indirect language also softens requests and refusals: 'I am not sure that will work' may mean no. Listen for tone and context, not only words.

Examples:
How was the exam? Not bad, actually. (It went very well.)
It is a bit chilly today. (It is minus twenty.)
I am not sure Friday works for me. (Friday does not work.)

Try it: Listen for understatement or indirect refusals this week and write down three examples with what the speaker probably meant.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Politeness strategies
lessons.body:
Learn: Polite English often softens directness: 'Would you mind...?', 'I was wondering if...', and 'Perhaps we could...' all make requests easier to accept. The more you ask of someone, or the less well you know them, the more indirect the language usually becomes. Over-politeness, though, can confuse: clarity still matters.

Examples:
Would you mind closing the window?
I was wondering if you could review this report by Friday.
Perhaps we could meet next week to discuss the plan.

Try it: Turn four direct orders into polite requests using different softening phrases. Then decide which version is clearest, not just politest.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Preparing to negotiate
lessons.body:
Learn: Preparation decides most negotiations. Know your goal, your minimum acceptable outcome, and your best alternative if talks fail. Research the other side's interests, not only their stated position: a landlord who refuses a lower rent might accept a longer lease or earlier payment.

Examples:
My goal is a rent of $1,300. My minimum is $1,400.
My alternative is a smaller apartment nearby.
The landlord wants reliable, long-term tenants, which I can offer.

Try it: Prepare for a negotiation you may face: goal, minimum, alternative, and two interests the other side may hold. Write them down before any meeting.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Persuasive language
lessons.body:
Learn: Persuasion combines logic, credibility, and emotion, but in professional settings logic and evidence carry most weight. Use data, precedent, and shared interests: 'Last year, similar buildings...' is stronger than 'I feel this is unfair.' Concede a small point to gain credibility on a larger one.

Examples:
Last year, three similar apartments on this street rented for $1,250.
I have paid on time for two years and kept the unit in good condition.
I understand costs have risen, and I am open to a twelve-month lease.

Try it: Write a persuasive paragraph for a rent discussion using one fact, one precedent, and one concession. Keep it under 100 words.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Handling objections
lessons.body:
Learn: Objections are information, not rejection. Listen fully, restate the concern to show you understood, and answer the real worry behind it. If you cannot answer at once, say so honestly and promise a specific follow-up time. Rushing past an objection usually makes it return stronger.

Examples:
You are worried the schedule change will burden evening staff.
Let me check the numbers and come back to you by Thursday.
If the burden is real, we can adjust the plan together.

Try it: Role-play an objection: one person raises a concern, the other restates it, answers it, and offers a follow-up. Swap roles and try a harder objection.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Closing an agreement well
lessons.body:
Learn: A good close confirms what both sides agreed, in plain language, and in writing. Summarize the terms, the dates, and each side's next steps, and thank the other party. Written confirmation prevents most later disputes, which usually come from memory, not bad faith.

Examples:
To confirm: rent of $1,350 from June 1, for twelve months, with parking included.
I will sign the updated lease by Friday.
Thank you for working through this with me.

Try it: Write a confirmation message for a fictional agreement: terms, dates, next steps for each side, and thanks. Keep it short enough to send by email.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Summarizing research
lessons.body:
Learn: A research summary states the question, the method in brief, the main finding, and its limits. Avoid copying sentences: restate ideas in your own words and name the source. A summary that omits limits misleads readers, however accurate its other sentences are.

Examples:
The study asked whether evening classes improve language retention.
It followed 120 adult learners for six months.
Evening learners retained 15% more vocabulary, but the sample was small and urban only.

Try it: Summarize a short research article in four sentences: question, method, finding, and one limit. Then check that no sentence copies the original wording.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Citing sources honestly
lessons.body:
Learn: Citations show where ideas came from and let readers verify them. Cite any idea, number, or quotation that is not your own, and distinguish your interpretation from the source's claim. Paraphrasing without a citation is still using someone else's work, even with different words.

Examples:
According to Statistics Canada (2024), the city's population grew by 3%.
This growth, I argue, explains pressure on rental housing.
The number is the source's; the explanation is mine.

Try it: Write a paragraph using two sources: cite each claim, then add one sentence of your own interpretation, clearly marked as yours.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Seminar discussion skills
lessons.body:
Learn: Seminars reward participants who build on others' ideas. Use phrases such as 'Building on Sara's point...', 'That raises a question...', and 'I would challenge that reading because...'. Refer to the text by page or section, and invite quieter voices in rather than dominating the discussion.

Examples:
Building on Sara's point about funding, the data on page 12 supports her claim.
That raises a question: does the same pattern hold in rural areas?
I would challenge that reading, because the author's sample excludes small towns.

Try it: Practise three seminar moves on a short text: building on a point, raising a question, and respectfully challenging a reading, each with a text reference.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Abstracts and executive summaries
lessons.body:
Learn: An abstract compresses a longer work into its essentials: purpose, method, key results, and conclusion, usually in under 250 words. An executive summary adds a recommendation for decision-makers. Both must stand alone: a reader who reads only the summary should grasp the whole argument.

Examples:
Purpose: To test whether mentorship helps newcomer job seekers.
Method: Interviews with 30 participants over one year.
Result: Mentored job seekers found work two months sooner on average.
Conclusion: Fund mentorship in settlement programs.

Try it: Write a 100-word abstract for a report you know well: purpose, method, result, and conclusion. Then cut it to 50 words without losing the conclusion.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Telling your story in English
lessons.body:
Learn: A personal story told well connects across cultures. Choose one moment, set the scene briefly, show what changed, and end with what it means to you now. Details make stories vivid: a place, a sound, a small decision. Avoid explaining every cultural reference; let the story carry its meaning.

Examples:
When I arrived in January, snow was falling and I had never seen it.
My neighbour brought soup and showed me how to dress for minus thirty.
That evening I understood that winter here is survived together, not alone.

Try it: Write a 150-word story about one moment in your Canadian life: scene, change, and meaning. Read it aloud and cut any sentence the story does not need.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Discussing culture with sensitivity
lessons.body:
Learn: Cultural discussions need curiosity and care. Ask open questions, avoid generalizing about whole groups, and describe practices you have observed rather than assuming motives. If you make a mistake, apologize simply, learn, and move on: most people value honest interest over perfect wording.

Examples:
I noticed families gather differently here than in my home country.
Could you tell me more about how holidays work in your family?
Thank you. I did not know that, and I appreciate you explaining it.

Try it: Write three open, respectful questions about a cultural practice you are curious about. Check each one: does it generalize, or does it ask about experience?

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Canadian history in plain language
lessons.body:
Learn: Canada's history includes Indigenous peoples who have lived here for thousands of years, French and British settlement, Confederation in 1867, and waves of immigration that continue today. Learning this history, including its difficult chapters such as residential schools, helps newcomers understand the country they now call home.

Examples:
Indigenous peoples lived on these lands long before European arrival.
Confederation united several colonies into Canada in 1867.
Newcomers continue to shape Canada's cities, workplaces, and culture.

Try it: Summarize one chapter of Canadian history in five sentences, in your own words. Then write one question you would like to explore further.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Adapting without losing yourself
lessons.body:
Learn: Adapting to a new country does not mean abandoning who you are. Many newcomers blend languages, foods, holidays, and values from two homes, and raise children who move between cultures. Naming what you keep, what you change, and why gives you control over the process.

Examples:
At home we speak Arabic and cook the food I grew up with.
At work I speak English and follow Canadian workplace customs.
My children move between both worlds, and I am proud of that.

Try it: Write three sentences: one thing you keep from your first culture, one thing you have adopted here, and one thing you are still deciding. Keep it honest and personal.

categories.name: English level C2
categories.description: Mastery English: precise, flexible English for complex topics.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Present simple
lessons.body: Learn: Use present simple for habits, routines, and facts. For I, you, we, and they, use the base verb: I work, they live. For he, she, and it, add -s or -es: She works, He watches. Examples: I wake up at seven. She wakes up at seven. We live in Winnipeg. He lives in Winnipeg. The bus stops here every day. Try it: Say three sentences about your routine. Use one sentence with he or she, and remember the -s: for example, My sister works in a shop.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Present simple
lessons.body: Learn: Use do and does to make questions and negatives. I, you, we, they use do. He, she, it use does, and then the verb has no -s. Examples: Do you speak English? Does she speak English? I do not work on Sunday. He does not work on Sunday. Try it: Ask a friend: Do you live near here? Then answer for another person: No, she does not live near here. Practice again: Say the examples out loud, slowly, then write them in your notebook. Repeat each new word three times, and use it in a new sentence about your own day in Canada.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Present simple
lessons.body: Learn: Use time words with present simple: always, usually, sometimes, never, every day, on Monday. Examples: I always eat breakfast. She usually walks to school. They never drive at night. We go to the library every Saturday. Try it: Write four sentences about your week. Use always, usually, sometimes, and never, one in each sentence. Practice again: Say the examples out loud, slowly, then write them in your notebook. Repeat each new word three times, and use it in a new sentence about your own day in Canada.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Present simple
lessons.body: Learn: Be careful with spelling: verbs ending in -y after a consonant change y to i and add -es: study becomes studies, try becomes tries. Verbs ending in -s, -x, -ch, or -sh add -es: watch becomes watches. Examples: She studies English. He tries a new word every day. The teacher watches the class. My friend fixes the chair. Try it: Change these verbs for he: study, try, watch, fix. Then say a full sentence with each one.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Present continuous
lessons.body: Learn: Use present continuous for actions happening now, or around now. Form: am, is, or are + verb + -ing. I am reading. She is reading. They are reading. Examples: I am writing now. He is cooking dinner. We are learning English this year. The baby is sleeping. Try it: Look around you. Say three things happening now, for example: I am sitting. My friend is talking. Practice again: Say the examples out loud, slowly, then write them in your notebook. Repeat each new word three times, and use it in a new sentence about your own day in Canada.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Present continuous
lessons.body: Learn: Use is not and are not, and am not, for negatives. I am not working today. She is not watching TV. They are not playing now. Examples: It is not raining now. He is not driving today. We are not studying at night. Try it: Say two things you are not doing now, and two things a friend is not doing now. Practice again: Say the examples out loud, slowly, then write them in your notebook. Repeat each new word three times, and use it in a new sentence about your own day in Canada.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Present continuous
lessons.body: Learn: Use present continuous for plans in the near future, especially with a time word: tomorrow, tonight, on Friday. Examples: I am meeting my teacher tomorrow. We are going to the library tonight. She is visiting her family on Friday. Try it: Tell a friend two plans for this week. Use tomorrow or on Friday in each sentence. Practice again: Say the examples out loud, slowly, then write them in your notebook. Repeat each new word three times, and use it in a new sentence about your own day in Canada.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Present continuous
lessons.body: Learn: Some verbs are not usually used in continuous form, because they describe a state, not an action: know, like, love, want, need, understand. Examples: I know the answer. She likes tea. We want help. Do not say: I am knowing the answer. Try it: Say five sentences with know, like, love, want, and need. Do not add -ing to these verbs. Practice again: Say the examples out loud, slowly, then write them in your notebook. Repeat each new word three times, and use it in a new sentence about your own day in Canada.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Past simple
lessons.body: Learn: Use past simple for a finished action in the past. Regular verbs add -ed: walk becomes walked, work becomes worked. Use a past time word: yesterday, last week, last year. Examples: I walked to school yesterday. She worked last Saturday. They lived in Toronto last year. Try it: Tell a friend what you did yesterday, in three sentences. Use yesterday in the first sentence. Practice again: Say the examples out loud, slowly, then write them in your notebook. Repeat each new word three times, and use it in a new sentence about your own day in Canada.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Past simple
lessons.body: Learn: Many common verbs are irregular in past simple: go becomes went, eat becomes ate, see becomes saw, have becomes had, buy becomes bought. Examples: We went to the park. I ate lunch at noon. She saw her friend. He bought a book. Try it: Say five sentences about last weekend. Use went, ate, saw, had, and bought, one in each sentence. Practice again: Say the examples out loud, slowly, then write them in your notebook. Repeat each new word three times, and use it in a new sentence about your own day in Canada.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Past simple
lessons.body: Learn: Use did to make past questions and negatives. After did, use the base verb, not the past form: Did you go? I did not go. Examples: Did she call you? No, she did not call me. Did they work yesterday? They did not work yesterday. Try it: Ask a friend three questions about yesterday. Start each one with Did you, and answer with did or did not. Practice again: Say the examples out loud, slowly, then write them in your notebook. Repeat each new word three times, and use it in a new sentence about your own day in Canada.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Past simple
lessons.body: Learn: Be careful with spelling: verbs ending in -e add only -d: live becomes lived. Verbs ending in -y after a consonant change y to i and add -ed: study becomes studied. Examples: He lived here last year. She studied English in the evening. We danced at the party. I closed the door. Try it: Write the past form of live, study, dance, close, and carry. Then say a sentence with each past form. Practice again: Say the examples out loud, slowly, then write them in your notebook. Repeat each new word three times, and use it in a new sentence about your own day in Canada.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Past continuous
lessons.body: Learn: Use past continuous for an action in progress at a time in the past. Form: was or were + verb + -ing. I was reading at eight. They were reading at eight. Examples: She was cooking at six. We were walking in the park. It was raining yesterday morning. Try it: Think about yesterday at eight in the evening. Say what you were doing, and what a family member was doing. Practice again: Say the examples out loud, slowly, then write them in your notebook. Repeat each new word three times, and use it in a new sentence about your own day in Canada.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Past continuous
lessons.body: Learn: Use past continuous with past simple to show a long action and a short action that interrupted it. The long action uses was or were + -ing. The short action uses past simple. Examples: I was walking home when it started to rain. She was reading when the phone rang. They were playing when their teacher arrived. Try it: Write two sentences like this: one long action, and one short action with when. Use was or were in the long part.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Past continuous
lessons.body: Learn: Use while for two actions happening at the same time in the past. Both parts can use past continuous. Examples: While I was cooking, he was cleaning the kitchen. While she was studying, her brother was watching TV. Try it: Tell a friend what two people were doing at the same time yesterday evening. Start with While. Practice again: Say the examples out loud, slowly, then write them in your notebook. Repeat each new word three times, and use it in a new sentence about your own day in Canada.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Past continuous
lessons.body: Learn: Use was not and were not for negatives. I was not sleeping at ten. She was not working last night. They were not driving in the rain. Examples: He was not listening to music. We were not playing outside. It was not snowing yesterday. Try it: Say three things you were not doing last night, and one thing a friend was not doing. Practice again: Say the examples out loud, slowly, then write them in your notebook. Repeat each new word three times, and use it in a new sentence about your own day in Canada.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Present perfect
lessons.body: Learn: Use present perfect to connect the past and now. Form: have or has + past participle. I have lived here for two years. She has lived here for two years. Examples: I have studied English since January. He has worked in this shop for one year. We have lived in Canada since 2024. Try it: Say one sentence about yourself with have or has, and for or since. For example: I have lived here for one year.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Present perfect
lessons.body: Learn: Use have or has + past participle for life experience, with ever or never. The exact time is not important. Examples: I have visited Toronto. She has never visited Vancouver. Have you ever taken a bus in Canada? Yes, I have. Try it: Ask a friend: Have you ever cooked a new food? Then answer with have or have not, and one place you have visited. Practice again: Say the examples out loud, slowly, then write them in your notebook. Repeat each new word three times, and use it in a new sentence about your own day in Canada.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Present perfect
lessons.body: Learn: Use just, already, and yet with present perfect. Just means a very short time ago. Already means before now. Yet is used in questions and negatives, at the end.
