Examples: I have just finished my homework. She has already eaten lunch. Have you finished yet? No, I have not finished yet. Try it: Say three sentences: one with just, one with already, and one question with yet. Practice again: Say the examples out loud, slowly, then write them in your notebook. Repeat each new word three times, and use it in a new sentence about your own day in Canada.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Present perfect
lessons.body: Learn: Do not use a finished past time word like yesterday or last week with present perfect. Use present perfect with for, since, just, already, yet, ever, and never. Examples: Correct: I have lived here since January. Not correct: I have lived here yesterday. Correct past simple: I lived here last year. Try it: Fix these sentences if needed: I have watched a film yesterday. She has worked here since June. They have played football last week.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Past perfect
lessons.body: Learn: Past perfect talks about an earlier past action before another past action. Form: had + past participle. Use it to show order in the past, for example when one thing happened before another thing. Examples: I had eaten lunch before my friend arrived. She had finished her homework before the lesson started. Try it: Say two sentences about yesterday, using had + a past participle in the first one, for example: I had read the book before I watched the film.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Past perfect
lessons.body: Learn: Past perfect is often used with before, after, and by the time. It helps the listener know which action came first. Examples: By the time I got home, my brother had cooked dinner. After I had washed my hands, I ate my lunch. Try it: Practise with before: I had studied English before I moved to Canada. Now make your own sentence with by the time.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Past perfect
lessons.body: Learn: Do not use past perfect for a single past action with no earlier action. Use past simple for that action, and past perfect only for the earlier one. Examples: I watched a film yesterday. (past simple, one action) I had watched the film before, so I knew the story. (past perfect for the earlier action) Try it: Choose the right form: I ___ (see) the shop before I went there again. Answer: had seen.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Past perfect
lessons.body: Learn: Past perfect questions use Had + subject + past participle. Short answers are Yes, I had. / No, I had not. Examples: Had you visited Winnipeg before you moved here? Yes, I had. / No, I had not. Try it: Ask a friend: Had you studied English before today? Listen for a short answer, then say a full sentence about it.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Future forms
lessons.body: Learn: Future forms talk about later time. Common forms are will, going to, and present continuous for plans. The choice depends on how sure you are and whether it is a plan or a decision now. Examples: I will call you tomorrow. We are meeting the teacher on Monday. Try it: Say three future sentences: one with will, one with going to, and one with present continuous for a plan.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Future forms
lessons.body: Learn: Use will for a quick decision, a promise, or an offer. Use going to for a plan you already made, or for something you can see happening. Examples: I will help you with your bag. We are going to visit the library tomorrow. We already planned it. Try it: Practise: I will open the door for you. (offer) / I am going to study tonight. (plan) Now make one offer and one plan.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Future forms
lessons.body: Learn: Present continuous for the future is used for fixed plans with a time, often with a person or place. It is not used for a general prediction. Examples: I am seeing a doctor on Friday at ten. They are travelling to Toronto next week. Try it: Make a fixed plan: I am meeting ___ on ___ at ___. Fill in a person, a day, and a time.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Future forms
lessons.body: Learn: Will not is won't, and going to is often shortened in speech to gonna, but write going to in school work. Check the time word: tomorrow, next week, on Monday, soon. Examples: I won't be late tomorrow. She is going to start a new job next month. Try it: Write four future sentences, each with a different time word: tomorrow, next week, on Friday, soon.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Going to and will
lessons.body: Learn: Going to shows a plan or something you can predict from what you see now. Will shows a decision made now, a promise, or a general future fact. Examples: Look at the clouds. It is going to rain. I will phone you tonight, I promise. Try it: Say a plan with going to, and a promise with will, for example: I am going to study tonight. I will help you tomorrow.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Going to and will
lessons.body: Learn: Going to + verb is: am/is/are + going to + verb. Will + verb is: will + verb, for all people, with no change for he, she, or it. Examples: He is going to buy a bus ticket. She will buy a bus ticket too. Try it: Practise the forms: I am going to read. He is going to read. They will read. Now say the same three forms about cooking.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Going to and will
lessons.body: Learn: For predictions, going to is strong when you see evidence now. Will is used for opinions and general predictions without clear evidence. Examples: The bus is late. It is going to be a long wait. I think it will be cold tomorrow. Try it: Look outside and make a going to prediction, then make a will opinion, for example: It is going to snow. It will be cold.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Going to and will
lessons.body: Learn: Questions: Are you going to study tonight? / Will you study tonight? Short answers: Yes, I am. / No, I'm not. / Yes, I will. / No, I won't. Examples: Are you going to visit the library? Yes, I am. / No, I'm not. Try it: Ask a friend two questions, one with going to and one with will, and listen for short answers.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Articles a, an, the
lessons.body: Learn: A and an are used for one, general thing. Use an before a vowel sound (a, e, i, o, u sound), and a before other sounds. The is used for a specific thing both people know. Examples: I have a pen. (one general pen) I have an apple. (an before a vowel sound) Try it: Say a or an for these: book, orange, house, egg. Answers: a book, an orange, a house, an egg.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Articles a, an, the
lessons.body: Learn: Use the when there is only one of something, or when you talked about it before. Do not use the for general plural ideas. Examples: The sun is hot today. (only one sun) I saw a dog. The dog was black. (the second time) Try it: Practise: I bought a book. The book is about Canada. Now tell a short story with a first, then the.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Articles a, an, the
lessons.body: Learn: No article is used for general plural nouns, school subjects, sports, and most meals. Use the for specific places like the library, when you mean a known place. Examples: I like apples. (general) I go to the library on Mondays. (a known place) Try it: Say three general ideas with no article, for example: I like music. I study English. I play football.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Articles a, an, the
lessons.body: Learn: Watch out for a and an with sounds, not letters. An hour starts with a vowel sound, so it is an hour. A university starts with a y sound, so it is a university. Examples: I waited an hour. She goes to a university in Winnipeg. Try it: Choose a or an: hour, university, umbrella, car. Answers: an hour, a university, an umbrella, a car.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Countable and uncountable nouns
lessons.body: Learn: Countable nouns can be counted: one book, two books. Uncountable nouns cannot be counted as single items: water, rice, money, information. Use some, any, much, many, and a lot of in the right way. Examples: I have some books. I need some water. Try it: Sort these into countable and uncountable: apple, milk, chair, bread. Answers: countable: apple, chair; uncountable: milk, bread.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Countable and uncountable nouns
lessons.body: Learn: Use many with countable nouns and much with uncountable nouns, usually in questions and negatives. Use a lot of with both in positive sentences. Examples: How many books do you have? How much water do you need? / I have a lot of books and a lot of water. Try it: Ask: How many friends do you have? How much time do you have? Answer with a lot of if you can.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Countable and uncountable nouns
lessons.body: Learn: Some uncountable nouns can be counted with a container or a piece: a bottle of water, a cup of coffee, a piece of bread, a piece of information. Examples: I want a bottle of water. She gave me a piece of advice. Try it: Say what you want with a container: a cup of tea, a bottle of milk, a piece of cake.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Countable and uncountable nouns
lessons.body: Learn: Some nouns change meaning: paper can be uncountable (material) or countable (a newspaper). Hair is usually uncountable, but a hair can mean one strand. Examples: I need some paper to write on. I read a paper this morning. (a newspaper) Try it: Practise: I need paper. (material) / I bought a paper. (newspaper) Now make two sentences with paper in both ways.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Pronouns and possessives
lessons.body: Learn: Pronouns replace nouns: I, you, he, she, it, we, they. Possessives show ownership: my, your, his, her, its, our, their. Use the right pronoun for the person or thing. Examples: I am Sara. She is my friend. This is my book. It is mine. Try it: Say: I am ___. This is my ___. He is my friend. His name is ___.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Pronouns and possessives
lessons.body: Learn: Subject pronouns come before the verb, object pronouns after the verb or a preposition: me, you, him, her, it, us, them. Examples: I help him with English. The teacher talks to us every day. Try it: Practise: I see her. She sees me. Now make two sentences with him and us.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Pronouns and possessives
lessons.body: Learn: Possessive adjectives come before a noun, possessive pronouns stand alone: my book / mine, your book / yours, his book / his, her book / hers. Examples: This is your pen. That pen is yours. Our house is small. Theirs is bigger. Try it: Choose: This is ___ (my/mine) bag. Answer: my. Then say: This bag is mine.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Pronouns and possessives
lessons.body: Learn: Use its for things, not it's, which means it is. Use their for people or things, not there, which means a place. Examples: The cat is eating its food. Their books are on the table. Try it: Correct these: It's food is here. / There books are new. Answers: Its food is here. / Their books are new.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Adjectives and adverbs
lessons.body: Learn: Adjectives describe nouns: big, small, happy, new. They usually come before the noun, or after be, look, feel, seem. Examples: I have a new book. The book is new. Try it: Describe three things near you with an adjective, for example: a big bag, a warm coat, a happy dog.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Adjectives and adverbs
lessons.body: Learn: Adverbs describe verbs, adjectives, or other adverbs. Many adverbs end in -ly: slowly, quickly, carefully. They often come after the verb or before an adjective. Examples: She speaks slowly. He drives carefully. Try it: Make sentences: I walk slowly. I speak carefully. Now say how you study, with an -ly adverb.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Adjectives and adverbs
lessons.body: Learn: Adjectives do not change for plural nouns, and adverbs do not change for he, she, or they. Good is an adjective, well is usually an adverb. Examples: They are good students. She speaks English well. Try it: Choose good or well: She is a ___ student. She studies ___. Answers: good, well.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Adjectives and adverbs
lessons.body: Learn: Some adverbs of frequency come before the main verb, but after be: always, usually, often, sometimes, never. Examples: I usually study in the morning. She is always on time. Try it: Say how often you study: I always / usually / sometimes / never study in the evening. Pick the true one for you.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Comparatives and superlatives
lessons.body: Learn: Comparatives compare two things: bigger, smaller, more interesting. For short adjectives, add -er. For long adjectives, use more + adjective. Use than to compare. Examples: Winnipeg is bigger than my town. English is more difficult than my first language. Try it: Compare two places you know: ___ is bigger than ___. / ___ is more beautiful than ___.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Comparatives and superlatives
lessons.body: Learn: Superlatives compare three or more things, or a group: the biggest, the most interesting. Use the before a superlative. Examples: This is the biggest library in the city. She is the most helpful teacher. Try it: Say: The ___ is the biggest ___ in my city. Fill in the words for a place you know.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Comparatives and superlatives
lessons.body: Learn: Spelling changes: big becomes bigger and biggest, happy becomes happier and happiest, good becomes better and best, bad becomes worse and worst. Examples: This book is better than that book. Today is the worst day for rain. Try it: Practise: good, better, best. Bad, worse, worst. Now compare two books with better and best.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Comparatives and superlatives
lessons.body: Learn: Use as + adjective + as to say things are equal, and not as + adjective + as to say they are not equal. Examples: My bag is as big as yours. Her English is not as fast as mine yet. Try it: Make equal and unequal comparisons: My room is as big as yours. My room is not as big as the living room.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Prepositions of place and time
lessons.body: Learn: Prepositions of place tell where: in, on, at, under, next to, between, behind, in front of. In is for inside a place, on is for a surface, at is for a point or address. Examples: The book is on the table. I live at 123 Main Street. Try it: Say where things are: My phone is on the table. My bag is under the chair. Now describe your room.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Prepositions of place and time
lessons.body: Learn: Prepositions of time tell when: in for months, years, and morning/afternoon/evening, on for days and dates, at for times and night. Examples: I study in the morning. The lesson is on Monday at ten. Try it: Practise: I was born in ___. My lesson is on ___. I sleep at ___. Fill in your own time words.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Prepositions of place and time
lessons.body: Learn: Next to means beside, between means in the middle of two things, behind means at the back, in front of means at the front. Examples: The bank is next to the library. The shop is between the bank and the school. Try it: Describe your street: The ___ is next to the ___. The ___ is between the ___ and the ___.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Prepositions of place and time
lessons.body: Learn: Do not use in for a specific day, or on for a month. Check the time word first: in June, on June 5, at 5 p.m., in the morning, on Monday morning. Examples: I will visit in June. I will visit on June 5 at noon. Try it: Choose in, on, or at: ___ Monday, ___ June, ___ 9 a.m. Answers: on Monday, in June, at 9 a.m.

courses.title: Modal verbs can, could, may, might

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Modal verbs can, could, may, might
lessons.body: Learn: Can talks about ability and permission now. Could talks about ability in the past, and polite requests now. May and might talk about possibility, and may is also polite permission. Examples: I can speak English. Can I use your pen, please? Try it: Say what you can do, and ask politely: I can read English. Can I borrow your book, please?

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Modal verbs can, could, may, might
lessons.body: Learn: Modal verbs do not change for he, she, or it, and they are followed by a verb with no to: He can swim. She might come. Not: He cans swim. / She might to come. Examples: He can cook well. She might visit tomorrow. Try it: Correct these: He can speaks English. / She mights come. Answers: He can speak English. / She might come.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Modal verbs can, could, may, might
lessons.body: Learn: Negative forms: cannot or can't, could not or couldn't, may not, might not. Questions: Can you help me? / Could you help me? Could is more polite than can for requests. Examples: I can't swim yet, but I can read. Could you help me, please? Try it: Ask politely: Could you open the door, please? Then answer: Yes, of course. / Sorry, I can't.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Modal verbs can, could, may, might
lessons.body: Learn: May and might are similar for possibility, but might is a little less sure. Use may for formal permission, for example in a letter or at school. Examples: It may rain tomorrow. It might rain tomorrow, but I am not sure. Try it: Say a possibility: It may be cold tomorrow. / I might go to the library. Then say which one you are more sure about.

courses.title: Modal verbs must, should, have to

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Modal verbs must, should, have to
lessons.body: Learn: Must talks about a strong rule or something you are sure about. Should talks about advice. Have to talks about a rule from outside, like a school or a job. Examples: You must wear a seatbelt in a car. You should study every day. Try it: Say a rule with must, advice with should, and a job rule with have to, for example: I must show my card. I should sleep early. I have to be on time.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Modal verbs must, should, have to
lessons.body: Learn: Must not means it is not allowed. Do not have to means it is not necessary, but it is allowed. This is a common mistake, so check the meaning. Examples: You must not smoke here. You don't have to bring food. We have food. Try it: Choose: You ___ bring a pen. It is not necessary. Answer: don't have to. Then say: You must not be late.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Modal verbs must, should, have to
lessons.body: Learn: Questions: Must I come? / Do I have to come? / Should I come? Must is formal, have to is common, should asks for advice. Examples: Must I bring my passport? Should I bring my passport? Try it: Ask three questions: Must I ___? Do I have to ___? Should I ___? Fill in a real task, like study or come early.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Modal verbs must, should, have to
lessons.body: Learn: In the past, had to is used for must and have to. Should have + past participle talks about a past mistake or missed advice, but use it carefully and simply. Examples: I had to wait yesterday. I should have studied more. Try it: Say: Yesterday I had to ___. Now make a simple past advice sentence: I should have ___.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Conditionals zero and first
lessons.body: Learn: Zero conditional talks about facts that are always true: If + present simple, present simple. First conditional talks about a real future possibility: If + present simple, will + verb. Examples: If you heat water, it boils. If it rains tomorrow, I will stay home. Try it: Make a fact and a future plan: If I study, I learn. If I study tonight, I will pass the test.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Conditionals zero and first
lessons.body: Learn: In first conditional, the if part uses present simple, not will. The result part uses will. You can swap the order, but keep the same verb forms. Examples: If you call me, I will help you. I will help you if you call me. Try it: Correct this: If you will call me, I will help you. Answer: If you call me, I will help you.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Conditionals zero and first
lessons.body: Learn: Use unless to mean if not: Unless you study, you will not pass. Unless is followed by a positive verb, not a negative one. Examples: Unless it rains, we will go to the park. I will come unless I am sick. Try it: Say: Unless I am busy, I will ___. Then say the same idea with if not: If I am not busy, I will ___.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Conditionals zero and first
lessons.body: Learn: Zero conditional is for science and general truths. First conditional is for plans and warnings. Check if the result is always true, or only in the future. Examples: If you mix red and blue, you get purple. If you don't eat, you will be hungry. Try it: Make two sentences: one always true, one future: If I press this button, the light turns on. If I press it tomorrow, I will see the light.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Conditionals second and third
lessons.body: Learn: Second conditional talks about an unreal present or future situation: If + past simple, would + verb. It is not about the past, it is about a dream or an unreal idea now. Examples: If I had more time, I would study more. If I lived in Toronto, I would visit the library every day. Try it: Make a dream sentence: If I had ___, I would ___. Fill in something you wish for.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Conditionals second and third
lessons.body: Learn: Third conditional talks about an unreal past: If + past perfect, would have + past participle. It talks about a past that did not happen, and a different result. Examples: If I had studied more, I would have passed. If I had left earlier, I would not have missed the bus. Try it: Say a past regret simply: If I had ___, I would have ___. Use a real small example, like left early or studied.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Conditionals second and third
lessons.body: Learn: Second and third conditionals use would, not will. Would have is for the past, would is for the present or future dream. Do not mix will into the if part. Examples: If I won the lottery, I would travel. If I had won the lottery, I would have travelled. Try it: Practise: If I had money, I would buy a car. If I had had money, I would have bought a car. Say both slowly.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Conditionals second and third
lessons.body: Learn: Questions: What would you do if you had more time? / What would you have done if you had known? Short answers can be simple: I would study. / I would have studied. Examples: What would you do if it rained tomorrow? I would stay home. Try it: Ask a friend: What would you do if you had a free day? Listen, then say: If I had a free day, I would ___.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Passive voice
lessons.body: Learn: Passive voice is used when the action is more important than who did it, or when we do not know who did it. Form: be + past participle. The subject receives the action. Examples: The room is cleaned every day. The letter was sent yesterday. Try it: Change to passive: People clean the room every day. Answer: The room is cleaned every day.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Passive voice
lessons.body: Learn: Present simple passive: am/is/are + past participle. Past simple passive: was/were + past participle. Future passive: will be + past participle. Examples: English is spoken in Canada. The house was built in 2001. Try it: Practise: The book is read by many students. The book was read last week. The book will be read next week.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Passive voice
lessons.body: Learn: Use by + person only when the person is important. Often we leave by out in passive sentences, especially in instructions and news. Examples: The cake was made by my mother. The road is closed today. (no by, person not important) Try it: Say two passive sentences without by, for example: The door is locked. The homework is checked every day.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Passive voice
lessons.body: Learn: Active voice is better when the person is important and clear: My mother made the cake. Passive is better when the action or result is the focus, like in a report or a rule. Examples: Active: The teacher checked the homework. Passive: The homework was checked. Try it: Choose active or passive: The teacher is important, so use active. The result is important, so use passive. Now make one of each.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Reported speech
lessons.body: Learn: Reported speech talks about what someone said, without quoting exact words. When the reporting verb is in the past, verbs often move back one step: present becomes past, past becomes past perfect. Examples: She said, I am happy. -> She said she was happy. He said, I live in Winnipeg. -> He said he lived in Winnipeg. Try it: Report: I am tired. Answer: She said she was tired. Now report: I live in Canada.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Reported speech
lessons.body: Learn: Pronouns and time words change too: I becomes he or she, my becomes his or her, here becomes there, today becomes that day, tomorrow becomes the next day. Examples: I will come tomorrow. -> He said he would come the next day. I am here today. -> She said she was there that day. Try it: Report: I will help you tomorrow. Answer: He said he would help me the next day.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Reported speech
lessons.body: Learn: Reported questions use if or whether for yes/no questions, and the question word for wh- questions. The word order becomes like a statement, not a question. Examples: Are you happy? -> He asked if I was happy. Where do you live? -> She asked where I lived. Try it: Report: Where are you from? Answer: He asked where I was from. Now report: Do you speak English?

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Reported speech
lessons.body: Learn: Reported commands use told + person + to + verb, and told + person + not to + verb for negatives. Said is used without a person, told is used with a person. Examples: Open the door. -> She told me to open the door. Don't be late. -> He told me not to be late. Try it: Report: Study every day. Answer: She told me to study every day. Now report: Don't forget your book.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Questions and question words
lessons.body: Learn: Question words ask for different information: who for a person, what for a thing, where for a place, when for a time, why for a reason, how for a way, which for a choice. Examples: Who is your teacher? Where do you live? Try it: Ask and answer: Who is your friend? What is your job? Where are you from? When is your lesson? Why do you study English?

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Questions and question words
lessons.body: Learn: Yes/no questions start with be, do, or a modal: Are you ready? Do you speak English? Can you help me? Wh- questions start with a question word, then be, do, or a modal. Examples: Are you from Canada? What do you do? Try it: Make a yes/no question and a wh- question about your day, for example: Do you study today? What do you study today?

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Questions and question words
lessons.body: Learn: In questions, the subject comes after be, do, or a modal: Where are you? / What do you want? In a statement, the subject comes first: You are here. / You want tea. Examples: Where is the library? The library is there. Try it: Change to a question: You are happy. Answer: Are you happy? Now change: You live in Winnipeg. Answer: Where do you live?

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Questions and question words
lessons.body: Learn: Prepositions can come at the end of a question in everyday English: Who are you talking to? What are you looking for? In formal writing, the preposition can come first, but everyday English is fine for class. Examples: Who are you waiting for? What are you thinking about? Try it: Ask: Who are you talking to? What are you looking at? Answer with a person or a thing.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Gerunds and infinitives
lessons.body: Learn: Gerunds are verb + -ing used as a noun: swimming, reading, studying. Infinitives are to + verb: to swim, to read, to study. Some verbs take a gerund, some take an infinitive, and some take both with a different meaning. Examples: I like swimming. I want to swim. Try it: Say: I like reading. I want to read. Now say what you like doing, and what you want to do.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Gerunds and infinitives
lessons.body: Learn: Common gerund verbs: enjoy, like, love, hate, finish, avoid, practise. Common infinitive verbs: want, need, decide, plan, hope, learn, try. Examples: I enjoy reading. I decided to study English. Try it: Practise: I enjoy ___. I want to ___. I decided to ___. Fill in real verbs for you.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Gerunds and infinitives
lessons.body: Learn: After a preposition, use a gerund, not an infinitive: I am good at swimming. Thank you for helping me. After an adjective, use an infinitive: It is easy to learn. I am happy to help. Examples: She is interested in learning English. It is difficult to speak fast. Try it: Correct: I am good at swim. Answer: I am good at swimming. Now say: I am happy to help you.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Gerunds and infinitives
lessons.body: Learn: Some verbs change meaning: I stopped smoking means I quit. I stopped to smoke means I stopped another activity in order to smoke. Remember means remember to do in the future, and remember doing in the past. Examples: I remembered to call her. I remember calling her yesterday. Try it: Say: I remembered to study. (future task) / I remember studying yesterday. (past memory) Notice the difference.
